title: Laredo Port Named in 21-Defendant Cartel Racketeering Indictment
excerpt: A federal grand jury in Del Rio indicted 21 alleged members of La Nueva Familia Michoacana; prosecutors say one defendant tried to move firearms through the Laredo Port of Entry in 2021.
content:
A federal grand jury in Del Rio has indicted 21 defendants in a 14-count racketeering case tied to the Mexican cartel La Nueva Familia Michoacana, and the Laredo Port of Entry is named in the allegations, federal prosecutors announced Friday, Nov. 20.

U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons for the Western District of Texas announced the indictment at a Homeland Security Task Force press conference in San Antonio. Prosecutors say brothers Johnny Hurtado Olascoaga, 53, known as “El Pez,” and Jose Alfredo Hurtado Olascoaga, 42, known as “El Fresa,” lead the cartel, which the United States designated a foreign terrorist organization on Feb. 20, 2025.

The charges include racketeering conspiracy, drug trafficking, firearms trafficking, alien smuggling, international money laundering, and providing material support to a designated foreign terrorist organization. Prosecutors allege the group has conspired since 2006 to import and distribute thousands of kilograms of cocaine, heroin, and methamphetamine, and that a migrant-smuggling count stems from the death of a minor in March 2021.

The Laredo connection comes in the firearms counts. According to the U.S. Attorney’s Office, defendants Edgar Aguilar Cruz and Rogelio Estrada Jaramillo conspired beginning in June 2020 to smuggle firearms, magazines, and ammunition from the United States into Mexico, including a .50-caliber rifle, seven 7.62-caliber rifles, an AR-15 rifle, a 12-gauge shotgun, and nearly 1,500 rounds of ammunition. Prosecutors allege Estrada attempted to export firearms to Mexico through the Laredo Port of Entry on or about Sept. 30, 2021.

Five of the 21 defendants are in federal custody: Jesus Daniel Alvarez, Alejandro Diaz Garcia, Rogelio Ponce Esquivel, Apolonio Benitez, and Omar Sixto Benitez. The other 16 are at large and believed to be in Mexico, according to prosecutors. If convicted, the defendants face penalties ranging from 10 years to life in federal prison and fines of up to $10 million.

An indictment is only an allegation, and all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty in court.

Source: U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Texas; KGNS.
